blocks.heading: Worker participation
blocks.text: Worker participation means employees contribute to decision-making in the business. The contribution can range from making suggestions or discussing changes to representation in a formal consultative arrangement. It differs from merely receiving a decision already made without opportunity to influence it. Participation does not necessarily transfer ownership or make every management decision a vote. Explain what workers can influence and how management responds. Staff knowledge can improve decisions, but involvement must be genuine and its limits clear.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Oru Packaging asks operators to help choose a new layout before management finalises it. Operators can contribute practical experience while the employer retains the stated final responsibility. Announcing the chosen layout afterwards without hearing staff would be communication but not the same participation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Participation, conflict and representation
blocks.text:
Fictional Tuli Print has a recurring machine-quality problem confined to one line. Operators understand it and management has time to investigate. It compares a quality circle with a representative council covering all departments.

Evaluate a quality circle against a worker council for Tuli’s original machine problem. Give a concise plan. [12]

Issue: a recurring technical-quality problem confined to one line. Quality circle: operator knowledge, focused investigation and practical proposals; requires time, data and a response. Council: broad representation is useful for wider policies but may add irrelevant complexity here. Conflict can worsen if staff are excluded or proposals ignored. Judgement: choose the circle for this focused issue, with management assessing proposals and reporting decisions. Use a wider representative method if the decision affects departments beyond the line.
